entries.title: Sleep paralysis · REM awakening
entries.summary: REM muscle atonia can persist briefly after cortical wake-up, leaving awareness with immobile limbs.
entries.reviewed_title: Sleep paralysis at awakening: what REM atonia can explain
entries.reviewed_description: Sleep paralysis can occur when awareness returns while REM-related muscle atonia briefly persists. Learn what the experience can and cannot tell you.
entries.search_intent: Explain temporary inability to move at awakening without turning sleep paralysis, chest pressure, or hallucinations into a dream diagnosis.

evidence_sections.established: Sleep paralysis is a dissociated sleep–wake state in which awareness can return while REM-related skeletal-muscle atonia persists briefly into wakefulness.
evidence_sections.supported_hypothesis: Irregular sleep schedules, sleep loss, and disrupted sleep can increase susceptibility in some people. Hallucination-like experiences, sensed presence, fear, and chest-pressure sensations may accompany an episode.
evidence_sections.unknown_or_limitation: A single episode does not reveal the meaning of a dream, identify a specific psychological cause, or by itself diagnose narcolepsy, REM sleep behavior disorder, or another neurological disorder.

observable_facts: Whether voluntary movement was temporarily impossible
Approximate duration of immobility
Whether unusual visual, auditory, or sensed-presence experiences occurred
Whether breathing felt difficult even though respiration continued
Whether the episode occurred while falling asleep or waking
entries.safety_boundary: Occasional isolated sleep paralysis is often benign. Recurrent distressing episodes, marked daytime sleepiness, cataplexy-like symptoms, unusual injuries, or other persistent sleep symptoms warrant clinical assessment.

citations.label: Recurrent Isolated Sleep Paralysis — Sleep Medicine Clinics (2024)

entries.title: Hypnic jerk · N1 onset
entries.summary: A transient motor burst during wake-to-N1 transition, often paired with a falling percept and brief arousal.
entries.reviewed_title: Hypnic jerks at sleep onset: sudden body jolts during the transition to sleep
entries.reviewed_description: Hypnic jerks are brief involuntary movements around sleep onset and are usually benign. Falling sensations or a sudden jolt do not identify a precise brain mechanism.
entries.search_intent: Explain a sudden jerk or falling sensation while drifting to sleep without assigning a fixed EEG, neurotransmitter, or symbolic meaning.

evidence_sections.established: Hypnic jerks, also called sleep starts, are brief involuntary movements that occur around the transition from wakefulness to sleep and are commonly benign.
evidence_sections.supported_hypothesis: Sleep loss, stress, or other factors that destabilize the transition to sleep may make sleep starts more noticeable in some people, but the exact trigger for an individual event is often uncertain.
evidence_sections.unknown_or_limitation: A falling sensation, limb jerk, or brief startle cannot identify a specific neurotransmitter change, exact EEG frequency, or hidden meaning of accompanying imagery.

observable_facts: Whether the movement was a single jerk or repeated series
Which part of the body moved
Whether a falling or startle sensation accompanied it
Whether the event immediately caused full awakening
Whether episodes are occasional or frequent
entries.safety_boundary: An occasional sleep start is generally benign. Frequent repetitive jerks, events occurring well outside sleep onset, injury, loss of awareness, or other concerning neurological symptoms deserve medical evaluation.

citations.label: Hypnic Jerks: A Scoping Literature Review — Sleep Medicine Clinics (2015)
The neurophysiologic landscape of sleep onset: a systematic review (2023)

entries.title: Hypnagogic tachycardia · N1
entries.summary: Sympathetic tone can surge while cortical activity drifts into theta-range hypnagogia.
entries.reviewed_title: Racing heartbeat at sleep onset: what a hypnagogic palpitation can and cannot show
entries.reviewed_description: Heart rate and autonomic activity change across the wake-to-sleep transition, but a racing-heart sensation does not identify N1, a neurotransmitter surge, or an arrhythmia.
entries.search_intent: Explain a brief racing-heart or palpitation sensation while falling asleep without treating hypnagogic tachycardia as a distinct sleep diagnosis.

evidence_sections.established: Cardiovascular and autonomic activity change dynamically across sleep and wakefulness, and sleep onset is a gradual, heterogeneous physiological transition rather than a single sharply defined event.
evidence_sections.supported_hypothesis: A brief awareness of a faster heartbeat near sleep onset may accompany an arousal or transition in autonomic state, but the same sensation can have many sleep-related and non-sleep-related causes.
evidence_sections.unknown_or_limitation: A racing-heart sensation cannot identify the exact sleep stage, demonstrate a norepinephrine or orexin surge, or distinguish normal autonomic variation from a cardiac rhythm disturbance.

observable_facts: Approximate duration of the racing-heart sensation
Whether the rhythm feels regular or irregular
Whether dizziness, faintness, chest pain, or shortness of breath occurs
Whether stimulants, medications, or recent sleep loss may be relevant context
How frequently the event recurs
entries.safety_boundary: Persistent or recurrent palpitations, an irregular rhythm, fainting, chest pain, significant shortness of breath, or symptoms occurring outside the sleep transition should be medically assessed.

citations.label: The neurophysiologic landscape of sleep onset: a systematic review (2023)
Autonomic regulation during sleep and wakefulness: review (2018)

entries.title: REM atonia failure · mid-cycle
entries.summary: Incomplete inhibitory drive to spinal motor neurons during REM allows fragmentary movement.
entries.reviewed_title: REM sleep without atonia: RSWA, movement during REM, and the RBD distinction
entries.reviewed_description: REM sleep without atonia is an objective EMG finding during REM sleep. RSWA alone is not the same as REM sleep behavior disorder.
entries.search_intent: Explain increased muscle activity during REM while distinguishing normal twitches, objectively measured RSWA, dream enactment, and REM sleep behavior disorder.

evidence_sections.established: REM sleep normally includes marked reduction of skeletal-muscle activity. REM sleep without atonia, or RSWA, refers to increased tonic or phasic muscle activity during REM measured with polysomnography and electromyography.
evidence_sections.supported_hypothesis: RSWA is an important physiological feature in REM sleep behavior disorder, but isolated RSWA can also be detected without the full clinical syndrome and does not have one uniform meaning in every person.
evidence_sections.unknown_or_limitation: A twitch, vocalization, or remembered movement cannot by itself diagnose RSWA or REM sleep behavior disorder. Dream content does not measure muscle atonia.

observable_facts: Whether movements are small isolated twitches or complex dream-enactment behaviors
Whether punching, kicking, grabbing, or leaving the bed occurs
Whether vocalizations accompany the movements
Whether the person or bed partner has been injured
Whether behavior is recurrent
entries.safety_boundary: Repeated dream enactment, punching, kicking, falls, or injury during sleep should be evaluated by a sleep specialist. Diagnosis of REM sleep behavior disorder requires clinical assessment and objective sleep evidence, not a dream report alone.

citations.label: Quantification of REM sleep without atonia: review and meta-analysis (2023)
REM Sleep Behavior Disorder: Clinical Presentation and Diagnostic Criteria (2024)
Isolated RSWA and isolated RBD: clinical and prognostic differences (2025)

entries.title: Sleep bruxism · N2
entries.summary: Rhythmic masticatory muscle activity often clusters around N2 with sigma-range spindle context.
entries.reviewed_title: Sleep bruxism: jaw-muscle activity during sleep
entries.reviewed_description: Sleep bruxism is rhythmic or non-rhythmic masticatory muscle activity during sleep. Jaw soreness or tooth wear alone cannot determine its sleep stage or cause.
entries.search_intent: Explain grinding, clenching, and jaw-muscle activity during sleep using current bruxism terminology without assigning a fixed N2, sigma, or dopamine mechanism.

evidence_sections.established: Sleep bruxism is masticatory muscle activity during sleep that can be rhythmic or non-rhythmic. Current consensus treats bruxism as a behavior that may have clinical consequences rather than automatically as a disease in every person.
evidence_sections.supported_hypothesis: Self-report, examination, and device-based measurements can contribute different levels of information about bruxism. Instrumental recordings provide stronger evidence about sleep-related muscle activity than symptoms alone.
evidence_sections.unknown_or_limitation: Morning jaw tension, tooth wear, or a report of grinding cannot by themselves identify the sleep stage, demonstrate a dopamine-driven mechanism, or establish why the activity occurred.

observable_facts: Whether grinding sounds are reported during sleep
Morning jaw-muscle fatigue, pain, or stiffness
Tooth wear, fractures, or dental damage
How frequently the behavior is noticed
Whether snoring or other sleep symptoms coexist
entries.safety_boundary: Persistent jaw pain, tooth damage, headaches, jaw locking, or suspected sleep-disordered breathing should be discussed with an appropriate dental or medical professional.

citations.label: Updating the Bruxism Definitions: International Consensus Meeting (2025)
Instrumental assessment of sleep bruxism: systematic review and meta-analysis (2024)

entries.title: Night sweats · N3
entries.summary: Thermoregulatory and sympathetic shifts during deep NREM can produce heavy sweating without full awakening.

entries.title: Hypnopompic surge · REM exit
entries.summary: As REM ends, rising aminergic tone can collide with residual cholinergic REM state, producing a body-wide surge.
entries.reviewed_title: Body sensations while waking: the hypnopompic transition
entries.reviewed_description: Brief jolts, unusual body sensations, or autonomic changes can occur while waking. The sensation alone does not prove REM, residual atonia, or a specific neural mechanism.
entries.search_intent: Explain unusual body sensations during awakening without presenting “hypnopompic somatic surge” as a standardized diagnosis.

evidence_sections.established: Awakening is a physiological state transition involving coordinated changes in brain activity and autonomic function. Hypnopompic sensory experiences can occur around the boundary between sleep and wakefulness.
evidence_sections.supported_hypothesis: A brief jolt, breath catch, racing heart, or unusual body sensation may accompany the arousal process, but the precise mechanism depends on the event and cannot usually be reconstructed from subjective recall alone.
evidence_sections.unknown_or_limitation: The experience does not establish that the person was in REM, that REM atonia partially failed, or that a particular aminergic or cholinergic switch produced the sensation.

observable_facts: The exact body sensation noticed during awakening
Approximate duration
Whether normal voluntary movement returned immediately
Whether palpitations or breathing difficulty occurred
Whether episodes recur and disrupt sleep
entries.safety_boundary: Brief isolated transition sensations may be benign. Recurrent severe episodes, loss of consciousness, persistent breathing difficulty, chest pain, seizure-like activity, or other concerning symptoms require medical assessment.

entries.title: Phasic REM eye bursts
entries.summary: Phasic REM packs ponto-geniculo-occipital-related bursts with rapid eye movements under preserved somatic atonia.

entries.title: K-complex micro-arousal · N2
entries.summary: High-amplitude K-complexes can mark protective or reactive cortical events with tiny somatic accompaniments.

entries.title: Sleep spindle density · N2
entries.summary: Thalamocortical sigma spindles gate sensory flow; somatic quietude often tracks dense spindle trains.

entries.title: Slow-wave stillness · N3
entries.summary: Delta-dominant N3 couples high homeostatic sleep pressure with low motor output.

entries.title: REM HRV constriction
entries.summary: Phasic REM can tighten beat-to-beat variability while skeletal atonia stays intact.

entries.title: Limb-float hypnagogia · N1
entries.summary: Proprioceptive drift in N1 can feel like floating as muscle tone and sensory gating shift.

entries.title: PLMS-like kicks · N2
entries.summary: Stereotyped leg movements can punctuate N2 with brief cortical arousals after each burst.
entries.reviewed_title: Periodic limb movements during sleep: PLMS, repeated leg movements, and PLMD
entries.reviewed_description: PLMS are repetitive stereotyped limb movements measured during sleep. Their clinical significance varies, and one remembered kick does not diagnose PLMS or PLMD.
entries.search_intent: Explain repeated leg movements during sleep while separating a subjective movement report from polysomnographic PLMS and periodic limb movement disorder.

evidence_sections.established: Periodic limb movements during sleep are repetitive, stereotyped sleep-related limb movements that can be quantified during polysomnography.
evidence_sections.supported_hypothesis: PLMS may coexist with restless legs syndrome and several other sleep, neurological, medical, or medication-related conditions. Their clinical relevance varies substantially between individuals.
evidence_sections.unknown_or_limitation: A remembered kick, bed-partner report, or isolated leg movement cannot establish the periodicity, movement index, associated arousals, or diagnosis of periodic limb movement disorder.

observable_facts: Whether movements appear repetitive and stereotyped rather than isolated
Whether a bed partner notices recurring leg or foot movements
Whether movements appear to disrupt sleep
Whether restless-leg sensations occur while awake before sleep
Whether there is meaningful daytime sleepiness or fatigue
entries.safety_boundary: Persistent repetitive movements accompanied by insomnia, daytime impairment, significant restless-leg symptoms, or another suspected sleep disorder should be assessed clinically. PLMS and PLMD are not interchangeable terms.

citations.label: Consensus roadmap on periodic leg movements during sleep — International PLMS Taskforce (2026)

entries.title: Onset breathing pause · N1
entries.summary: Respiratory drive can briefly wobble at sleep onset as chemoreflex and upper-airway tone reconfigure.
entries.reviewed_title: Breathing pauses at sleep onset: transition physiology versus sleep apnea
entries.reviewed_description: Breathing control changes as wakefulness gives way to sleep, and brief central pauses can occur near sleep onset. A felt pause or gasp cannot diagnose sleep apnea.
entries.search_intent: Explain a perceived breathing pause or gasp while falling asleep while clearly separating transition physiology from obstructive or central sleep apnea diagnosis.

evidence_sections.established: The transition from wakefulness to sleep changes respiratory control. Central breathing pauses can occur around sleep onset, while clinically significant central sleep apnea is defined by recurrent objectively measured events involving reduced or absent respiratory effort.
evidence_sections.supported_hypothesis: An isolated brief pause near sleep onset may reflect transient instability in respiratory control, but similar subjective sensations can occur for many reasons and cannot establish the type of respiratory event.
evidence_sections.unknown_or_limitation: A subjective breath-hold feeling, chest stillness, or gasp cannot distinguish central from obstructive apnea, determine oxygen levels, or diagnose a sleep-related breathing disorder.

observable_facts: Whether another person has witnessed repeated breathing pauses
Whether there is recurrent gasping or choking during sleep
Whether loud habitual snoring is present
Whether excessive daytime sleepiness is present
Whether the event is isolated or repeatedly disrupts sleep
entries.safety_boundary: Repeated witnessed apneas, recurrent gasping or choking, significant daytime sleepiness, or other signs of sleep-disordered breathing warrant formal clinical assessment. Severe breathlessness, chest pain, or an acute medical emergency requires urgent care.

citations.label: Update on the Pathophysiology, Aetiology and Management of Central Sleep Apnoea (2026)

entries.title: REM vascular engorgement
entries.summary: Autonomic REM physiology includes genital engorgement cycles independent of waking sexual context.

entries.title: Early-night N3 stillness
entries.summary: First-cycle slow-wave sleep often shows maximal stillness aligned with endocrine recovery windows.

entries.title: Fragmented REM micro-arousals
entries.summary: Interrupted REM shows mixed EEG and incomplete atonia as wake-promoting systems intrude.

entries.title: Alpha intrusion · N2
entries.summary: Alpha-range intrusion into NREM can leave the body still while subjective sleep feels shallow.

entries.title: Tonic REM stillness
entries.summary: Between phasic bursts, tonic REM holds skeletal atonia with theta-leaning cortical activity.

entries.title: Microsleep nod · N1
entries.summary: Seconds-long N1 intrusions produce postural collapse markers under high sleep pressure.

entries.title: N3 exit motor confusion
entries.summary: Forced exit from delta sleep can leave motor systems online while cortical clarity lags.
entries.reviewed_title: Confusional arousal: incomplete awakening from NREM sleep
entries.reviewed_description: Confusional arousals are disorders of arousal involving incomplete awakening from NREM sleep with confusion or disoriented behavior.
entries.search_intent: Explain confusion and slow or disoriented behavior during an incomplete awakening without pretending that the episode reveals an exact EEG frequency or neurotransmitter state.

evidence_sections.established: Confusional arousal belongs to the NREM disorders of arousal, in which elements of sleep and wakefulness coexist during an incomplete awakening. Episodes often arise from slow-wave sleep, although NREM stage distribution is not absolute.
evidence_sections.supported_hypothesis: Sleep disruption, sleep deprivation, and other factors that increase or destabilize arousals can contribute to disorders of arousal in susceptible people.
evidence_sections.unknown_or_limitation: A report of confusion, mumbling, or clumsy movement cannot reconstruct an individual's EEG, identify a specific transmitter change, or distinguish every parasomnia from seizures or other disorders.

observable_facts: Approximate duration of confusion after the apparent awakening
Whether speech or behavior was disorganized
How much of the event was remembered afterward
Whether complex behaviors such as walking occurred
Whether the event created a risk of injury
entries.safety_boundary: Frequent episodes, dangerous behavior, injury, new adult-onset events, or events that could represent seizures or another sleep disorder warrant clinical evaluation.

entries.title: REM temperature deregulation
entries.summary: Thermoregulatory responses are blunted in REM, so ambient shifts feel more abrupt somatically.

entries.title: Swallow burst · N2
entries.summary: Protective airway reflexes can fire in N2 with short-lived neck and laryngeal markers.

entries.title: Pre-REM atonia ramp · N2
entries.summary: Approaching REM, inhibitory drive to motor neurons ramps while EEG still shows N2 features.

entries.title: Awakening motor readiness · N1
entries.summary: Late-sleep lightening into N1/wake aligns endocrine rise with returning motor readiness.

entries.title: Sawtooth-wave REM onset
entries.summary: Sawtooth waves often herald REM entry as atonia consolidates and eye movements begin.

entries.title: N3 relative bradycardia
entries.summary: Deep NREM favors parasympathetic dominance and slower heart rate with minimal movement.

entries.title: Exploding-head burst · N1
entries.summary: A brief auditory/sensory bang at the wake–sleep border without external sound — a transition phenomenon.
entries.reviewed_title: Exploding head syndrome: a sudden sound sensation at the sleep–wake boundary
entries.reviewed_description: Exploding head syndrome involves a sudden perceived bang or explosive sound around a sleep transition. Its underlying mechanism remains uncertain.
entries.search_intent: Explain a sudden internal bang or explosive sound near sleep onset without inventing an EEG signature, neurotransmitter cause, or supernatural interpretation.

evidence_sections.established: Exploding head syndrome describes brief episodes in which a person perceives a sudden loud bang, explosion, or similar sensory event around a sleep–wake transition without a matching external sound.
evidence_sections.supported_hypothesis: Several neurological and sleep-transition mechanisms have been proposed, but current evidence does not establish one specific mechanism for all episodes.
evidence_sections.unknown_or_limitation: The experience does not demonstrate a glutamate surge, a specific EEG band, seizure activity, or a particular psychological meaning. The underlying pathophysiology remains incompletely understood.

observable_facts: What the perceived sound or sensory burst was like
Whether there was any matching external sound
Whether the event occurred while falling asleep or waking
Whether pain, weakness, confusion, or other neurological symptoms occurred
How often the episodes recur
entries.safety_boundary: Typical isolated episodes are usually brief and benign. A new severe headache, persistent pain, loss of consciousness, focal neurological symptoms, or seizure-like events require medical assessment rather than interpretation as exploding head syndrome.

citations.label: Exploding Head Syndrome: A Systematic Scoping Review — Sleep Medicine Clinics (2024)

entries.title: Distal REM twitches
entries.summary: Phasic REM allows brief distal motor breakthroughs while proximal atonia largely holds.

entries.title: Fragmented REM with micro-arousals · theta 4.04–10.17 Hz · REM
entries.summary: Fragmented REM with micro-arousals, scattered across broken stage fragments maps onto [brief body shifts · dry mouth on wakelets · micro-arousal body hitch] inside theta 4.04–10.17 Hz, atonia "partial_failure" — read as mechanism, not dream-symbol shorthand.
entries.reviewed_title: Fragmented REM sleep: repeated arousals, awakenings, and what they can show
entries.reviewed_description: REM sleep can be interrupted by arousals and awakenings. Subjective broken sleep or fragmented dream recall cannot by itself prove REM fragmentation.
entries.search_intent: Explain REM fragmentation and REM instability without assigning synthetic EEG frequencies, transmitter profiles, or atonia scores to a subjective experience.

evidence_sections.established: REM sleep can be interrupted by arousals and awakenings, and REM arousal measures can be quantified during polysomnography. Increased REM instability has been studied in insomnia and other sleep conditions.
evidence_sections.supported_hypothesis: In some populations, greater REM instability may contribute to the experience of disrupted or non-restorative sleep, but it is not a universal explanation for fragmented sleep.
evidence_sections.unknown_or_limitation: Fragmented dream recall, dry mouth, body shifts, or repeated awakenings cannot establish that the interrupted stage was REM or reveal a specific EEG frequency, neurotransmitter pattern, or degree of atonia.

observable_facts: Number and timing of remembered awakenings
Whether dream recall appears as several separate fragments
Whether snoring, gasping, or choking accompanies awakenings
Medication, alcohol, stress, or schedule changes that coincide with the disrupted night
Whether daytime functioning is impaired
entries.safety_boundary: Persistent fragmented or non-restorative sleep, especially with snoring, gasping, witnessed apneas, chronic insomnia, or significant daytime impairment, warrants evaluation for the underlying cause rather than assuming REM fragmentation from subjective recall.

citations.label: Insomnia and REM sleep instability (2023)
